BEIRUT, Lebanon (CNN) -- Amid high emotions and tight security, thousands lined the streets of Beirut Friday to honor Antoine Ghanem, the anti-Syrian Lebanese MP killed in a powerful bomb blast along with four others. Amin Gemayel (R), Phalange party head, carries the coffin of assassinated deputy Antoine Ghamen. Against an atmosphere of intense political and patriotic fervor, the flag-draped coffins of the politician and two bodyguards also killed in Wednesday's rush hour blast made its way through the city's Christian district to the Sacred Heart church on what the government had declared as a day of national mourning. The procession was accompanied by thousands waving flags, as well as a brass band playing the anthem of Ghanem's Phalange Party, The Associated Press reported . TV pictures showed distraught mourners crowding and reaching out to the coffins as they were carried aloft. Several people were seen to collapse and had to be carried away. Mourners also carried photographs, threw rose petals and unfurled banners, some of which read "We Won't Kneel," AP said. The coffins were greeted at the Christian Maronite church with applause from the gathered mourners, the agency said, including majority leaders and the Lebanese cabinet as well as Ghanem's family and friends. Ghanem was later buried in the city's Christian district. Ghanem's death is the latest in a series of attacks targeting prominent anti-Syrian figures, with the most notorious being the February 2005 assassination in Beirut of former Lebanese Prime Minister Rafik Hariri, which sparked widespread protests that led to the ouster of Syrian forces from Lebanon. Hariri also died in a massive explosion. The incident threatens to cast the country into political uncertainty ahead of a key presidential vote in a tightly divided parliament, almost evenly split between anti- and pro-Syrian camps.  Watch how Ghanem's death disrupts Lebanese politics » . CNN's Beirut bureau chief Brent Sadler said that many Lebanese now feared for the future, especially given other events in the region including the conflict between Palestinians and Israelis, recent political differences in Iraq and Iran's bid to become a super power. "There continues to be among a great deal of people here a sense of foreboding that perhaps the worst is yet to come," he said. U.S. President George W. Bush, in a written statement, joined other world leaders in condemning the "horrific assassination." "Since October 2004, there has been a tragic pattern of political assassinations and attempted assassinations designed to silence those Lebanese who courageously defend their vision of an independent and democratic Lebanon," Bush said Wednesday. Also in a written statement, a spokesperson for Ban Ki-moon said the U.N. secretary-general "condemns in the strongest terms this terrorist attack." "The secretary general urges all Lebanese to exercise utmost calm and restraint at this very critical time and to allow judicial procedures to take their course," the spokesperson said. Bush's statement added: "The United States opposes any attempts to intimidate the Lebanese people as they seek to exercise their democratic right to select a president without foreign interference. We will continue to stand shoulder-to-shoulder with the Lebanese people as they resist attempts by the Syrian and Iranian regimes and their allies to destabilize Lebanon and undermine its sovereignty." The U.S. Embassy in Beirut issued a statement saying: "It is not a coincidence that these attacks target those figures who have been working to secure Lebanon's independence from renewed Syrian hegemony. We note with concern that many Lebanese politicians allied with Syria have in fact warned that murder and violence would be the results of any effort to exercise genuine parliamentary democracy." And U.S. Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice, in a written statement, said: "The bombing that claimed these lives was another act in a campaign of terror by those who want to turn back the clock on Lebanon's hard-won democratic gains." "The world should speak with one voice in calling for an end to violence in Lebanon intended to subvert democratic processes in that country," Rice said. "Lebanese elections, scheduled to begin in just days, must proceed, in accordance with the Constitution, without threats of foreign interference and the violence that accompanies such obstruction." **BEIRUT, Lebanon (CNN)** — Thousands of people gathered under heavy security in Beirut on Friday to pay tribute to Antoine Ghanem, an anti-Syrian member of Lebanon’s parliament who was killed with four other people in a powerful bombing.

Amin Gemayel, leader of the Phalange Party, helped carry Ghanem’s coffin. The caskets of Ghanem and two of his bodyguards, who also died in Wednesday’s rush-hour explosion, were covered with Lebanese flags and carried through Beirut’s Christian district to Sacred Heart Church. The government had designated Friday a national day of mourning.

The procession unfolded amid strong patriotic and political emotion. According to The Associated Press, thousands of participants waved flags while a brass band performed the Phalange Party anthem. Television footage showed grieving mourners pressing toward the raised coffins and trying to touch them. Several people collapsed and were carried from the crowd.

Participants held photographs, scattered rose petals and displayed banners, including some declaring, “We Won’t Kneel,” AP reported.

When the coffins reached the Maronite Christian church, the crowd greeted them with applause. Those present included leaders of Lebanon’s parliamentary majority, Cabinet members, and Ghanem’s relatives and friends. He was later buried in the Christian section of the city.

Ghanem’s killing was the newest in a succession of attacks against leading anti-Syrian figures. The best-known case was the February 2005 assassination of former Lebanese Prime Minister Rafik Hariri, who was also killed in a huge Beirut explosion. Hariri’s death triggered mass demonstrations that eventually forced Syrian troops to leave Lebanon.

The latest bombing raised the prospect of further political instability shortly before an important presidential election in Lebanon’s deeply divided parliament, where pro-Syrian and anti-Syrian blocs held nearly equal strength.

CNN Beirut bureau chief Brent Sadler said many Lebanese were anxious about what lay ahead. Their concern was intensified by other regional developments, including the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, recent political disputes involving Iraq, and Iran’s effort to establish itself as a superpower. Sadler said many people in Lebanon felt a strong sense of dread and believed conditions could become even worse.

In a written statement, U.S. President George W. Bush joined other international leaders in denouncing what he called the “horrific assassination.” Bush said Wednesday that, beginning in October 2004, Lebanon had experienced a tragic series of political killings and attempted killings intended to silence Lebanese citizens who bravely supported an independent, democratic country.

A spokesperson for U.N. Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon also released a statement saying Ban condemned the bombing in the strongest possible terms as a terrorist attack. The secretary-general called on all Lebanese citizens to remain as calm and restrained as possible during the critical period and to let the judicial process proceed.

Bush also said the United States rejected efforts to frighten the Lebanese people as they exercised their democratic right to choose a president free from outside involvement. He pledged continued U.S. support for Lebanon as its people opposed attempts by Syria, Iran and their allies to destabilize the country and weaken its sovereignty.

The U.S. Embassy in Beirut said the selection of victims was not accidental, arguing that the attacks had targeted people working to protect Lebanese independence from a renewed period of Syrian dominance. The embassy also expressed concern that several Lebanese politicians aligned with Syria had warned that attempts to practice genuine parliamentary democracy would lead to violence and murder.

U.S. Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice said in a separate written statement that the bombing was another episode in a terror campaign by forces seeking to reverse Lebanon’s hard-earned democratic progress. She urged the international community to unite in demanding an end to violence aimed at disrupting Lebanese democracy.

Rice added that Lebanon’s elections, due to start within days, should move forward under the Constitution and without foreign threats, interference or related violence.

**Lebanon Mourns Slain Lawmaker as Assassination Deepens Political Crisis**

**BEIRUT, Sept. 21, 2007** — Thousands of mourners filled the streets of Beirut on Friday for the funeral procession of Antoine Ghanem, an anti-Syrian member of Lebanon’s Parliament whose assassination two days earlier intensified fears that political violence could derail the country’s approaching presidential election.

Ghanem, a 64-year-old member of the Christian Phalange, or Kataeb, Party, was killed Wednesday when a powerful car bomb exploded in the predominantly Christian Beirut suburb of Sin el-Fil. At least six other people were killed and dozens were wounded in the blast, which tore through vehicles, storefronts and nearby buildings.

Mourners carrying Lebanese and Kataeb flags accompanied Ghanem’s flag-draped coffin as church bells rang. Supporters threw flowers and shouted slogans in favor of Lebanese sovereignty and against Syrian interference. Senior leaders of the Western-backed parliamentary majority joined members of Ghanem’s family at the funeral Mass, while security forces deployed heavily along the procession route.

The service became both an act of mourning and a political demonstration by the coalition known as the March 14 movement. Its leaders accused Syria and its allies of seeking to eliminate members of the parliamentary majority before lawmakers were due to begin choosing a successor to President Emile Lahoud, whose term was set to end in November.

Syria condemned the killing and denied involvement. No group immediately claimed responsibility.

Ghanem had returned to Lebanon only days before his death after spending much of the summer abroad because of security concerns. His killing reduced the governing coalition’s already narrow majority in the 128-seat Parliament and raised fears that further assassinations could alter the balance of power or prevent the legislature from reaching the quorum needed for a presidential vote.

The bombing followed a series of attacks against prominent anti-Syrian politicians and public figures that began with the February 2005 assassination of former Prime Minister Rafik Hariri. The resulting public protests and international pressure forced Syria to withdraw troops it had stationed in Lebanon for nearly three decades. But the withdrawal did not end the struggle between the March 14 coalition and a Syrian-backed opposition led by Hezbollah and its allies.

Other anti-Syrian figures killed in the ensuing campaign included journalist and legislator Gebran Tueni, former Communist Party leader George Hawi, journalist Samir Kassir and Industry Minister Pierre Gemayel, a senior Kataeb figure. Lawmaker Walid Eido was killed in another Beirut bombing in June 2007.

At Friday’s funeral, political leaders portrayed Ghanem’s death as part of the same campaign.

Former President Amin Gemayel, the Kataeb leader and father of Pierre Gemayel, called on the Lebanese people to resist intimidation and defend the country’s democratic institutions. Other March 14 leaders said Parliament must proceed with the presidential election despite the threat of violence.

The vote was especially contentious because Lebanon’s sectarian political system requires the president to be a Maronite Christian. The governing coalition and opposition disagreed over both the candidates and the constitutional rules governing the election. Opposition factions argued that a two-thirds quorum was required, while some majority leaders maintained that a president could ultimately be elected by an absolute majority.

The assassination drew immediate international condemnation.

U.S. President George W. Bush said he “strongly condemned” Ghanem’s murder and described it as part of an effort to intimidate Lebanon’s elected representatives. He said the Lebanese people deserved to live in freedom and security, without violence or foreign interference, and reaffirmed Washington’s support for Lebanon’s sovereignty and democratic government.

United Nations Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon said he was shocked by the bombing and condemned it “in the strongest terms.” His office said attempts to destabilize Lebanon through political violence were unacceptable and urged Lebanese leaders to preserve national unity and continue the constitutional political process.

U.S. Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice said the assassination appeared intended to influence Lebanon’s presidential election by frightening or eliminating members of Parliament. She said the Lebanese people and their elected representatives must not be intimidated and stressed that the election should take place free of outside interference.

The funeral unfolded under extraordinary security. Soldiers and police guarded intersections, searched vehicles and restricted traffic in areas surrounding the church and procession route. Many shops closed as a sign of mourning, while television stations broadcast the ceremony live.

For Ghanem’s supporters, the public turnout was meant to demonstrate that the campaign of bombings had failed to silence the anti-Syrian movement. But the procession also underscored the vulnerability of Lebanon’s political institutions. Each assassination had narrowed the governing coalition’s margin and deepened mistrust between rival factions.

As Ghanem was laid to rest, Lebanon faced the prospect of entering the presidential election period without a political compromise and with lawmakers increasingly fearful for their lives. The chants from the procession called for unity and independence, but the heavy security presence and the growing list of assassinated politicians reflected a country still caught between democratic politics and the threat of renewed violence.
